So Climate Action is a collaborative between local organizations, municipalities, and community members focused on climate change mitigation.

We are co-led by both Reap Green Solutions and Sustainable Waterloo Region as a collaborative partnership that is funded by the region, the three cities, and working collaboratively with all eight municipalities.
At a high level, we coordinate the activities of our climate action plans and strategies,
measure and monitor progress towards our climate emissions reductions targets, and engage the
community broadly in climate action initiatives.
So what brings me here today?
Back in 2013, we did our first community greenhouse gas inventory, and emissions came from five
sectors – transportation, workplaces, homes, agriculture, and waste.
led to Waterloo Region's first Climate Action Plan to achieve a 6% emissions
reduction from by the year 2020 based on 2010 baseline emissions. So that's
approximately an 842,000 ton reduction over seven years. So we are here today to
close the chapter on our first Community Climate Action Plan and report the
progress since we last came in 2017. In 2017 we released the first iteration of
our progress our path with the re-inventory using 2015 data and reported a 5.2 percent reduction
compared to the 2010 baseline year. We saw an increase in transportation emissions and decreases
in both homes and workplaces. The changes we saw were attributed largely to the closure of
provincial coal power plants as well as reduced consumption and increased efficiency in the areas
of homes and workplaces. Due to the abnormal circumstances in 2020 and the drastic effects
of the COVID-19 pandemic, we conducted a reinventory for two years, 2020 to account for the end
of the 6% target, and 2019 to look at a year that is more close to business as usual.
In 2019, we see that we maintain some of the emissions reduction from the 2010 baseline
year at 3.7%, and in 2020 a decrease of 14.4%, more than doubling the emissions reduction target
of 6%. Though 2019 does show us that without the drastic impacts of the pandemic, we would have
been unlikely to reach our 6% target in 2020. So looking a little closer, we continue to see that
the transportation of goods and people is the highest emitting sector, followed by the ICI
workplaces sector, and then homes in third. And while we did experience an upward trajectory of
our emissions since 2015, we are encouraged to see that the per capita emissions growth rate is not
the same as our population rate. So starting at 8.4 tons averaged per person in 2010,
down to 7.1, still lower than 2015, despite more absolute emissions.
So still a long way to go, but a few key takeaways from the report today.
It is since 2010 emissions, transportation emissions do remain the largest contributor
and continue to increase despite gains in fuel efficiency.
So it is essential that we change the ways we move both goods and people.
Energy efficiency, fuel switching, and local energy generation provide a significant opportunity
for transformational change across all sectors.
And there have been many promising initiatives that we're only beginning to see the greenhouse gas reduction benefits of.
We're encouraged by all of the stories that are throughout our full report and the many more that we weren't able to fit in the report.
So where are we going from here?
